OBITUARY REFERENCE 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon’ble Members, I refer with profound sorrow to the passing 
away of Shri Jagdish Prasad Mathur, a former Member of this House on the 4th August, 
2007, at the age of 80. 
Born at Sikar district of Rajasthan in J anuary, 1928, Shri Mathur had his education 
at Sikar and Law College, Jaipur. 
An advocate and a social worker, Shri Mathur was associated with various social 
welfare organisations. The legislative career of Shri Mathur started with the 
membership of the Rajasthan Legislative Assembly, where he was a Member from 1957 
to 1962. He represented the State of Rajasthan in this House from April, 1970 to April, 
1976. Shri Mathur was also a Member of the 6th Lok Sabha. 
In the passing away of Shri Mathur, the country has lost an able Parliamentarian and 
a noted social worker. 
We deeply mourn the passing away of Shri Jagdish Prasad Mathur. 
I request Members to rise in their places and observe silence as a mark of respect to 
the memory of the departed. 
[Hon. Members then stood in silence for one minute] 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Secretary -General will convey to the members of the bereaved 
family our deep sense of sorrow and sympathy. 
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: Banarsi Das Guptaji has also expired this morning.  
__________ 
REFERENCE TO VICTIMS OF TWIN BOMB BLASTS IN HYDERABAD 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon’ble Members, it is with utmost grief and sorrow that I refer 
to the tragic killing of more than 40 persons in the twin bomb blasts that occurred in 
Hyderabad on the 25th of August, 2007. More than 50 persons also reportedly got 
injured in these blasts. 

2       Submissions by [RAJYA SABHA] Members 
No words are strong enough to condemn this heinous act. The killing of so many 
innocent people has shocked the entire nation. Such mindless and heartless acts of 
terrorism need to be dealt with firmness and resolve. 
I am sure the whole House will join me in condemning this cowardly and senseless 
act and in offering condolences to the bereaved families and pray for early recovery of 
those who got injured in these blasts. 
I request Members to rise in their places and observe silence as a mark of respect to 
the memory of those who lost their lives in this tragedy. 
[Hon. Members then stood in silence for one minute]

SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, on 25th 
evening, between 7.00 p.m. and 8.00 p.m. there was a bomb blast just in front of the 
Secretariat, hardly 50 yards from the Secretariat, when people were witnessing a laser 
show at Lumbini Park in Hyderabad. Fifteen minutes later, another bomb blast took 
place near Gokul Chat Bhandar in Kothi, a busy locality in Hyderabad. In both the 
incidents, 42 people die d on that day and one more person died yesterday. In all, 43 
people died and more than 100 people got injured in that ghastly incident. Sir, prior to 
this incident, there was another incident in Mecca Masjid. It is a historical Masjid near 
Charminar. There was a bomb blast exactly 100 days prior to this incident wherein eight 
people died on the spot and six people died in the police firing. In all, 14 people died in 
the Mecca Masjid incident. Prior to that, there was another incident in 2005. A human 
bomb w as blasted just near the Police Task Force ACP office. On all the three 
occasions, the Government of Andhra Pradesh and the hon. Minister from Delhi visited 
the areas and said that they were investigating and people should remain cool and calm; 
people should support the Government and people should support whole -heartedly the 
steps taken by the Government. There was an assurance from the Central Government 
when the hon. Home Minister visited the Mecca Masjid and the hon. Chief Minister of 
Andhra Pradesh ass ured the people in Andhra Assembly that within three days people 
would be apprehended. That was the assurance when Mecca Masjid incident took place. 
We all supported the Government during that time. But what happened later on? Prior to 
this 25th blast, thr ee days earlier, there was a seizure of Rs.3 crore in a locality. Now, 
the Police are saying that there is a link between these two incidents. The activity of the 
Government is only post -mortem activity. There is no concrete step from the 
Government to prevent such incidents.

SHRI SITARAM YECHURY (West Bengal): Thank you, Sir. I rise today with a 
very heavy heart. I think, all of us have universally condemned this outrage. We have 
been subjected to such terrorist attacks whic h know no boundaries of any religion. It 
ought to be taken as an attack on our nation, on our country and on our people. In that 
spirit, Sir, certain issues must be compassionately addressed. I was in Hyderabad on the 
day the blasts took place. And, I was there at these venues soon after the blasts took 
place. At Lumbini Park, you cannot enter unless you pass through a metal detector and 
unless you pass your ticket through a slide on the basis of which the gate opens. Now, 
how could any terrorist enter that  place with a bomb? This is a question which needs to 
be answered and also the reckless manner in which even the security had been privatised 
by earlier Government and this Government. Public security cannot be put in the hands 
of private agencies, and that is one of the biggest reasons why this incident happened at 
Lumbini Park. I think, all the Governments are responsible for this. The earlier 
Government is as much responsible for taking this irresponsible step as is the present 
one. This needs to be immediately corrected. Otherwise, I do not think we will be able 
to check such lapses in future. 
Secondly, we have heard that this has happened on the 100th day of the blast at 
Mecca Masjid in Hyderabad. You had intelligence reports. Hyderabad was put on a hig h 
alert. For various reasons Hyderabad is being targeted. But despite all this, how did we 
allow this serial bombings to take place? These were not only two blasts planned on that 
day Sir. Four were planned, but mercifully two did not blow up. Otherwise, t he death 
toll could have been much larger. But, the serious intelligence lapses will have to be 
inquired into. The question is now not to apportion blame on anybody. That is not the 
issue. This is a serious concern for the country. And, the State Governmen t also will 
have to answer, despite warnings that had come from the Centre, why were necessary 
steps not taken? The country demands this answer. I do not subscribe to the fact that it is 
lack of any weakness or absence of a law that is preventing us from t aking action 
against such terrorists. We have had the law in the past. And, when you had the law, 
when you had the POTA, you had the Parliament being attacked. So, it is not a question 
of absence of any law. Let us not lull ourselves that if we have extra laws, we will be 
able to

DR. P.C. ALEXANDER (Maharashtra): Thank you very much, Sir, for giving an 
opportunity to an independent also to speak on the subject. I would like to place before 
the hon. House 6 points for consideration and action if they agree with them. The first 
point is that the subject of public ord er should be placed in the Concurrent List. I am 
saying this because I want to pre -empt my esteemed friend, the hon. Minister for Home 
Affairs, in his reply speech that ‘this is a subject of the State Government, I will violate 
the Constitution if I interf ere, I do not want to do it.’ We have reached a stage when the 
largest number of people killed as a result of terrorism anywhere in the world, is in our 
country. Things have reached such a serious stage that we cannot prolong the time for 
the inclusion of internal security and public order in the Concurrent List. 
Number two, there has to be a separate Internal Security Advisor in the Ministry of 
Home Affairs. I know the National Security Advisor is also responsible for internal 
security. But his hands are s o full with problems that he may not be able to devote the 
attention that this subject deserves. Therefore, a full -fledged, independent internal 
security officer, responsible to the Home Minister, has to be appointed. 
Thirdly, there has to be an Internal S ecurity Advisory Council with people with past 
experience in IB, RAW and other security organisations, and this Council should deal 
with this problem almost on a day-to-day basis, and not meet occasionally. 
Fourthly, you should create an Institute of inter nal Security Studies. We have a very 
useful Institute for Defence Studies which the Defence Minister makes use of in 
planning his action, planning for additional equipments etc. Like that, very urgently, 
consideration should be given for the creation of an Institute of studies on Internal 
Security. 
Fifthly, and that is the most important point, adequate resources should be kept at the 
disposal of the Ministry of Home Affairs. We now think in terms of supplying a jeep 
here, a mobile phone there for a Sub -Inspector. These things are not any longer 
important to the problem. When we are spending thousands and thousands of crores of 
rupees on defence, we should not grudge a few thousand crores for internal security. 
What happens to the country if internal security is allowed to drift down further? 
And finally, the Sixth point is, if some States are not capable of handling internal 
security, the Central Government should not hesitate to dismiss those Governments and 
appoint adequately experienced and strong people to manage the affairs of the State. 
Extortion is taking place; protection money is being given to these scoundrels in some 
parts of the country even by senior officers. I want these 6 suggestions to be very 
seriously considered. Out of the 6 consideration points, if at least, 3 or 4 points will 
meet with the approval of the Home Minister and the senior Members of the Cabinet, 
we can start a new chapter in meeting Internal security requirements.

SHRI ROBERT KHARSHIING (Meghalaya): Thank you, Mr. Chairman, Sir. 
Before I make my three brief points, allow me, Sir, to express my appreciation and, I am 
sure, on behalf of this whole House, that because of your intervention, we are having 
this debate today. Last Session, a number of us had met you, out of concern for the non-
functioning of this House, but, today, by your special intervention, we have been able to 
have this debate and all of us are grateful to you, Sir, for that. 
My first suggestion is, I agree with what my esteemed colleague who just now 
spoke, that we need to take an all -party attitude towards this very important issue and 
we need to build consensus. So, I would urge upon the hon. Home Minister to, perhaps, 
form an all-party Committee or to make a sort of some arrangement whereby all parties 
can offer their suggestions. 
The second point that I would like to make here, Sir, is, I am thankful that we have  
avoided,  as  I  listened  to  this  debate,  tarnishing  or  stereotyping  any

My third suggestio n, Sir, is, via this House, to the media, that let us avoid 
sensationalising or blowing things out of proportion. When we watched ‘2001 
September 11’ programmes, no blood- splattered bodies were shown; no gory pictures 
were shown during the London bombings,  but during the last few days, when we 
watched our television channels, it was very unfortunate that gory pictures of body parts 
were shown on our television channel. What does it. inculcate in our young people? It

take this opportunity to create a mountain out of a mole hill. I think, we are all aware 
that other things are happening in the country. Twenty- five million, as we speak, are 
displaced in Assam, U.P., Bihar, U ttarakhand and Orissa due to floods. Five hundred 
people died in Bihar and 1,500- 2,000 people died in East India, again, due to floods. 
While we are very serious about this issue, I think, we need to consider other matters 
also. Of the farmers who died in the last ten days, 14 are from Vidarbha. I appeal to all, 
while we are very concerned about this issue, that there are also other matters which we 
need to consider. Thank you. 
DR. BIMAL JALAN (Nominated): Thank you very much, Sir. I agree with most of 
what has been stated about the importance of this subject, naturally, as a citizen. I have 
one or two points to make. One, I don’t think that it is a question of amending the law or 
having a stricter law or TADA or POTA or even that of policy. It is a question  of 
instruments. I think, we need a complete turn around in the way in which we look at the 
whole issue of terrorism. It is a borderless world. We are talking about Nepal, Pakistan 
and so on. Our Constitution is old; it is of 1950. At that time, the law an d order was put 
in the State List. Here, I slightly agree or rather partially agree with Dr. Alexander, but 
not wholly. In a borderless and globalised world, not only in the economic sense but 
also in terms of terrorism, etc., what we need to do is to look  very closely at the 
distribution of powers between the Centre and the States, and we have to treat it on the 
same basis as the defence of the country. Anti -terrorism cannot be split as a concurrent 
subject or a State subject. You can have ordinary Law, an d order, the police kind of 
order, in the jurisdiction of a State, but I think, you have to put terrorism on the same 
basis as defence of the nation. Therefore, what is important is the instruments that are 
available, whether you create an institute here o r an institute there or councils, etc. They 
can be decided once you review the Constitutional provisions. This is a very important 
issue. We have made 104 Constitutional amendments and one more is necessary to 
define terrorism on the same basis as defence. This is the only suggestion which I would 
like to make to you for consideration. This is a very basic issue. I know it is a difficult 
issue, to have a dividing line between law and order and terrorism. But I hope it will 
receive the consideration of this august House. Thank you.

Fake encounters in J and K 
*221. SHRI JANARDHANA POOJARY: Will the Minister of DEFENCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that some innocent civilians were killed in fake encounters 
undertaken jointly by some officials of the Indian Army and the local police in J and K;  
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether a Committee has been set up to inquire into the matter; 
(d) if so, the  details thereof and the time -frame set for submission of the report by 
the Committee; and 
(e) the measures proposed to be taken by Government to ensure that such fake 
encounters do not take place and innocent civilians are not killed? 
THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI A.K. ANTONY): (a) to (e) The State of 
Jammu and Kashmir is facing the menace of militancy, aided and abetted from across 
the border, for quite some time. To counter the militancy in the State, Army and Central 
Para Military Forces have been deployed to assist the State administration. Army 
undertakes operations against the militants based on hard intelligence. In such 
operations, at times firings take place, especially when the militants are armed and they 
use fire arms against the force or innocent p ublic. Such encounters are unavoidable in 
the situation prevailing in the State. However, there are strict guidelines prescribed for 
the forces for honouring human rights during discharge of their duties. Dos and Don’t to 
be foIlowed while acting under Arm ed Forces Special Powers Act have also been laid 
down by the Army. The force personnel are also sensitized from time to time to 
discharge their duties with a humane face and with minimum inconvenience to the 
public. All reported cases of a alleged human ri ghts violations are investigated promptly 
by the Army and stringent punishments are awarded to those who are found guilty.  
During last 3 years (2005 onwards), four cases of alleged killing of civilian 
personnel by the Army in fake encounter have been repor ted. In all these four cases, a 
Court of Enquiry has been instituted and a number of witnesses have been examined. In 
two of the cases, criminal cases have been filed against some Army personnel in the 
district court by the State Police. 
The State Governme nt of J and K has also appointed a Commission of Enquiry on 
2nd April, 2007 to enquire into alleged fake encounters/custodial killings in the State 
and to give its report within six months. 
In order to sensitize the troops deployed in Counter Insurgency/Co unter terrorist 
operations, Human Rights Cells have been established at various levels. The  troops  are  
sensitized  at  regular  intervals  regarding  the  importance  of 

Written Answers to [29 AUG., 2007] Starred Questions     17 
upholding human rights  and avoiding collateral damage. Regular foundation and 
refresher training in human rights is also carried out.

Survey on Indian languages 
*226. SHRI B. J. PANDA: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is proposed to conduct a survey on Indian languages; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) when such last survey was conducted and what are its statistics? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI 
MANIKRAO GAVIT): (a) to (c) The First Linguistic Survey of India (LSI) was 
conducted by Sir George A. Grierson, an Irish philologist during 1898 -1927 in the pre -
independence period. The Survey results were published in 11 volumes and 19 parts 
establishing 544 dialects and 179 languages at that point of time. The LSI established 
for the first time six families of which these languages/dialects were affiliated in the 
undivided India. However, it (LSI) did not cover the Southern parts of India.  
The classification provided by LSI has been the basis for presentation of data on 
mother tongues/languages returned at each of the censu ses even in the post -
independence India. However, the affiliation of some of the languages in the 
classification has undergone a change based on subsequent investigations and research.  
Since LSI of Sir George A. Grierson has limitations arising out of the approach 
adopted then and since new tools, techniques and survey instruments for analysis and 
description of language have become available, the Government proposes to launch a 
New Linguistic Survey of India (NLSI). The NLSI project will be of 10 years dur ation 
and envisages an expenditure of more than Rs. 500 crores. For the Eleventh Plan, an 
expenditure of Rs. 280 crores is envisaged. 
Labour rights of women workers 
*227. SHRIMATI BRINDA KARAT: Will the Minister of LABOUR AND 
EMPLOYMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have any proposal to ensure the labour rights of women 
working in the unorganised sector; 

20     Written Answers to [RAJYA SABHA] Starred Questions 
(b) whether the Ministry has any plan to protect women in unorganised sector from 
tbe incidents of sexual harassment; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR AND 
EMPLOYMENT (SHRI OSCAR FERNANDES): (a) Several laws have been enacted 
to ensure labour rights of working women. Laws which are applicable to working 
women in the unorganized sector are Plantations Labour Act, 1951, the Contract Labour 
(Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970, Equal Remuneration Act, 1976, Minimum 
Wages Act, 1948, Inter -State Migrant Workers (Regulation of Employment and 
Conditions of Service) Act, 1979, the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961, the Building and 
Other Construction Workers (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) 
Act, 1996, Beedi Worker's Welfare Fund Act, 1976, Iron -Ore Mines, Manganese Ore 
Mines and Chrome Ore M ines Labour Welfare Fund Act, 1976, Mines Act, 1952, Lime 
Stone and Dolomite Mines Labour Welfare Fund Act, Mica Mines Labour Welfare 
Fund Act, 1946 etc. These laws regulate conditions and hours of work, provide creche 
facilities, time off for feeding children during working hours, maternity leave and 
separate toilets and washing facilities for female workers near the workplace.  
(b) and (c) The Hon’ble Supreme Court of India, in the case of writ petition No. 
666-70 of 1992 filed by Vishaka and Ors. Vs State of Rajasthan and Ors. has laid down 
certain guidelines for the prevention of sexual harassment of women employees in their 
work places. The Guidelines have the force of law under Article 141 of the Constitution 
of India. The guidelines provide for establi shment of a mechanism for redressal of 
complaints. 
Pursuant to the judgement of the Hon’ble Supreme Court, the issue was taken up 
with all the Central Ministries/Departments, the State Governments/Union Territories 
and Central Public Sector Undertakings (C PSUs) to constitute Complaints Committees 
and to implement the guidelines contained in the judgment in letter and spirit. 
Compliance reports in respect of setting up of Complaints Committees are being 
received from most of the Central Ministries/State Gove rnments/ Union 
Territories/Central Public Sector Undertakings (CPSUs). 
The Department of Personnel and Training issued a Notification on 02.11.1997 
amending the Conduct Rules applicable to the Central Government and the All India 
Services to the effect that sexual harassment at the work place constitutes a misconduct 
for which a Government Servant is liable for disciplinary action. 
With a view to making the guidelines applicable to employees in the private sector, 
necessary amendment has been carried out on  20.11.1999 to the Industrial Employment 
(Standing Orders) Act, 1946. Consequent upon this amendment, sexual harassment at 
the work place constitutes a misconduct for which a workman is liable for disciplinary 
action. Female workers in the unorganized sect or can raise an industrial dispute against 
sexual harassment through any registered trade union. A group of women workers can 
also raise a dispuhte by electing 5 representatives to represent in the conciliation 
proceedings by a general resolution.

ILO convention on fisheries and fisheries workers 
*231.   SHRI PRASANTA CHATTERJEE: 
SHRI TAPAN KUMAR SEN: 
Will the Minister of LABOUR AND EMPLOYMENT be pleased to state:  
(a) whether Government have ratified the IL O convention on fisheries and fisheries 
workers; and 
(b) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR AND 
EMPLOYMENT (SHRI OSCAR FERNANDES): (a) No, Sir. 
(b) The International Labour Conference of the ILO has only recently adop ted the 
Work in Fishing Convention, 2007 at its 96th Session held in Geneva in June, 2007. 
India voted in favour of the adoption. However, the certified copy of the adopted 
Convention has not yet been circulated to us by the Director General, ILO. Ratification 
of an ILO Convention is a voluntary process. In India, we ratify an ILO Convention 
only when the national laws and legislations are brought fully into conformity with the 
provisions of the Convention in question. A decision in respect of ratification is taken 
after due consultation with all stakeholders. This consultation process will start after 
ILO sends across the certified copy of the Convention.

Problem of drinking water 
*235.   SHRIMATI SUPRIYA SULE: 
SHRIMATI SHOBHANA BHARTIA: 
Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether UNDP’s Human Development Report 2006 focuses on one of the most 
serious problems facing humanity today the global water crisis as water supplies are 
under severe stress and more than a billion people have no access to sa fe drinking water 
and also two million children die every year for want of potable water and sanitation 
facilities; 
(b) whether India with a sixth of the world's population faces a rapidly growing 
water crisis, both in the urban and rural areas; and 
(c) if so, the steps Government propose to take in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI RAGHUVANSH PRASAD 
SINGH): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) Rural Drinking Water Supply is one of the six components of Bharat 
Nirman, which has been conceived as a plan to b e implemented in four years, from 
2005-06 to 2008- 09 for building rural infrastructure. Under Bharat Nirman, it is 
proposed to cover all uncovered habitations, slipped back habitations and quality 
affected habitations by 2008- 09. To achieve the above, the Central Government has 
increased the budget allocation from Rs. 2900 crore in 2004- 05 to Rs. 6500 crore in 
2007-08 in the rural drinking water sector. 
With regard to drinking water in urban areas, to supplement the efforts of the States, 
the Government of India has launched in December, 2005, a reform linked programme 
called Jawaharlal Nehru National Urban Renewal Mission (JNNURM) 

Written Answers to [29 AUG., 2007] Starred Questions     29 
under which additional assistance is made available to 63 selected cities including 
mega/metro cities, State capitals and other important cities for the development of 
integrated urban infrastructure including water supply and sanitation. A similar 
programme called Urban Infrastructure Development Schemes for Small and Medium 
Towns (UIDSSMT) has also been launched by Government of India for the 
improvement of drinking water supply in 5098 small and medium towns and cities (as 
per census 2001) not covered under JNNURM. 
Non-availability of LPT Ransar Valley in Shimla 
*236. S HRI RAJNITI PRASAD: Will the Minister of INFORMATION AND 
BROADCASTING be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that people of Ransar Valley in Shimla district of Himachal 
Pradesh are not getting the facility of Doordarshan programme due to non -availability 
of Low Power Transmitter (LPT); 
(b) whether it is also a fact that Government are ignoring the demands of people of 
Ransar Valley for installation of LPT; 
(c) whether there is any proposal of Government to install LPT so that people can 
avail the accessibility to Doordarshan programmes; and 
(d) if so, by when it will be installed? 
THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING (SHRI 
PRIYARANJAN DASMUNSI): (a) Yes, Sir, Ransar Valley does not get TV coverage 
from the nearby TV transmitter at Chirgaon due to hilly terrain in the area. 
(b) to (d) With the launch of free -to-air DTH service of Doordarshan ‘‘DD Direct 
Plus’’, all uncovered areas along with rest of the country (except A&N Islands) have 
been provided with multi channel TV coverage. DTH signals can be received a nywhere 
in the country, including Shimla district, with the help of small sized dish receive 
system. New transmitters are now not contemplated.

Pending cases of compensation to farmers 
*240. SHRl T.S. BAJWA: Will the Minister of DEFENCE be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of pending cases where compensation has not been paid yet to those 
farmers whose land was used for mining for defence purpose after the militant attack on 
Parliament; and 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor and number of farmers affected thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI A.K. ANTONY): (a) and (b) For 
occupation of lands during Operation Parakram, the number of farmers for whom 
compensation is yet to be released to Deputy Commiss ioners are approximately 790 in 
Districts Jammu and Poonch of J and K and Districts Gurdaspur and Ferozepur of 
Punjab. 
Government has sanctioned an amount of Rs.2,96,93,230/ - in June/July, 2007 for 
payment as compensation to approximately 684 farmers in Di stricts Ferozepur and 
Jammu. This amount will be placed shortly with concerned Deputy Commissioners by 
the Defence Estate officers. 
For the remaining cases in Districts Jammu, Poonch and Gurdaspur, the formalities 
for assessing/sanctioning of compensation are under way.

(d) the objectives to be achieved once the project is completed; and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF INDUSTRIAL POLICY 
AND PROMOTION, MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI ASHWANI 
KUMAR): (a) Government of India has accorded ‘in -principle’ approval to the ‘‘Delhi-
Mumbai Industrial Corridor’’ (DMIC) Project outline. The Concept Paper envisages the

instruments available for project funding.

domestic and foreign investment. It is expected that this will help in enhancing  
industrial activities, exports and employment.

completion of Delhi -Mumbai Dedicated Rail Freight Corridor Project. Second and

Misuse of funds by NGO’s 
†1737. SHRI LALIT KlSHORE CHATURVEDI: Will the Minister of HOME 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the complaints of misuse of funds received from foreign 
countries by vol untary organizations, especially organizations run by so called 
minorities are being received continuously; 
(b) if so, whether there is any system to examine the purpose of funds received from 
abroad with transparency; 
(c) whether provisions made in various Acts a gainst persons misusing such funds 
are proving effective; 
(d) whether Government would consider cancelling the recognition of those 
organizations against which complaints of using the funds for other purposes is found 
correct and to impose ban on them if they start activities with a new name; 
(e) whether such organizations are also getting amount through hawala; and 
(f) if so, mechanism to control the same? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI 
SHRIPRAKASH JAISWAL): (a) to (d) Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act [FCRA], 
1976, administered by the Ministry of Home Affairs, regulates the acceptance and 
utilisation of foreign contribution by association having a definite cultural, economic, 
educational, religious or social programme. The registration  or prior permission for 
acceptance of foreign contribution is granted to any association under FCRA, 1976 only 
after due verification of its activities and the antecedents of its functionaries. 
Complaints are received by the Ministry alleging misuse of fo reign contribution 
received by the associations. Such complaints are not restricted to associations run by 
minorities. As and when, any complaint relating to the violation of the provisions of the 
Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 1976 comes to the notice of the Government; 
appropriate action is taken under the Act. Monitoring of receipt and utilization of 
foreign contribution by associations is done through a scrutiny of the annual audited 
returns filed by the associations as well as through the inspe ction of accounts and 
records of the associations by the Monitoring Unit set up for the purpose. A facility for 
online submission of statutory annual returns has been introduced to facilitate better 
monitoring of the receipt and utilisation of foreign contribution. 
If any association is found involved in misutilisation/diversion of foreign 
contribution, action is initiated against the association. Such action include (i) placing 
the Association in the Prior Permission category, (ii) prohibiting it from rece iving 
foreign contribution, (iii) prosecuting it in a court of law or (iv) freezing its bank 
accounts. In case of serious violations, where it is found that the contribution is being 
diverted for purposes other than the stated objectives of the association , the matter is 
referred to Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) for a detailed investigation and 
prosecution, if necessary. There is no provision for cancellation of registration under the 
Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 1976.

Written Answers to [29 AUG., 2007] Unstarred Questions     91 
(b) whether this situation has further eroded public faith in police due to large 
pendency in police investigation of registered crimes and a significant number of 
investigations not resulting in charge-sheets; and 
(c) whether Government are considering separating law and order with which police 
claims to remain busy, and to strengthen prosecution by setting up a separate legal wing

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF  HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRIMATI V. RADHIKA SELVI): (a) to (c) (i) The Code of Criminal Procedure 
(Amendment) Bill, 2006 introduced in the Rajya Sabha on 23rd August, 2006 have 
following proposals for improving the conviction rate. 
(a) A new proviso to section 24(8) of  the Code of Criminal Procedure, 
1973 is proposed to be inserted to empower the Court to permit the victim 
to engage an advocate of his own choice to coordinate with the 
prosecution in consultation with the Central Government or the State

stages but may or do change in the course of time. If their statements are 
recorded by a Magistrate at the earliest opportunity, they are unlikely t o 
turn hostile. Therefore, a new section namely Section 164B Cr. P.C. is 
proposed to be inserted to provide that any police officer not below the 
rank of sub -inspector shall, in the course of investigation of any offence 
punishable with death or imprisonme nt for ten years or more, produce all 
persons whose statement appears to him to be material and essential for 
proper investigation of the case to the nearest Metropolitan Magistrate or

(ii) The Supreme Court vide its judgment dated 22.09.2006 in the WP No.

1757. DR. V. MAITREYAN: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to  
state: 
(a) the total estimated loss of life and property due to flash floods across the country 
in the current monsoon season, State-wise; 
(b) what immediate steps are being taken to provide relief and reh abilitation to the 
affected people in these States; 
(c) what is the total outlay for flood relief activities in these States; and 
(d) what measures are being considered to chalk out permanent protection for the 
people who are getting affected regularly due to the torrential rains? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRIMATI V. RADHIKA SELVI): (a) to (c) As per the information received from the 
State Governments and Union Territory, based on their preliminary assessment, 
estimated loss due to heavy rainsl floods/flash floods during South- west monsoon 2007, 
State-wise, are given in Statement-I (See below). 
The execution of the rescue and relief measures in the event of natural disasters is 
primarily the responsibility of the concerned State Governm ent. The distribution of 
relief on the ground is made by the concerned State. The Central Government  

Written Answers to [29 AUG., 2007] Unstarred Questions   103 
supplements  the efforts  of the State Governments by  providing  financial  and logistic 
support. 
The concerned State Governments have taken necessary rescue and relief operations 
in the affected areas which include evacuation of people to safer places, operation of 
relief camps and cattle camps and providing essential commodities viz. readymade food, 
wheat, rice, chura, Gur, salt, kerosene oil, shelter material like polythene sheets, etc. 
The State Governments also took necessary steps to prevent outbreak of any epidemic 
in the flood affected areas. 
Relief assistance in the wake of natural disast ers is provided through the Schemes of 
Calamity Relief Fund (CRF), which is contributed by the Government of India and the 
concerned State Governments in the ratio of 3:1. The State Level Committee under the 
chairmanship of Chief Secretary of the concerned  State is fully empowered to operate 
the CRF in accordance with the extant items and norms approved by the Government of 
India. Additional assistance is also provided in the wake of a calamity of severe nature 
from National Calamity Contingency Fund (NCCF) as per the laid down procedure. 
A Statement showing the allocation and release of Central Share of Calamity Relief 
Fund (CRF) and funds released from National Calamity Contingency Fund (NCCF) 
during the year 2007-08 is at Statement-II (See below). 
(d) The  Schemes for flood control are planned, funded and executed by the State 
Government concerned. The role of the Central Government is of a technical, catalytic 
and promotional nature. The Central Government has initiated various measures for 
assisting the States in the management of floods, which include:– 
(i) the setting up of the Rashtriya Barh Ayog in 1976 to look into the flood 
problem and suggest remedial measures. Based on its recommendations, 
flood management strategy in the country was formulated and  forwarded 
to all the concerned States; 
(ii) constitution of the Ganga Flood Control Commission in 1972 for the 
Ganga Basin States covering all the 23 river systems of Ganga; 
(iii) constitution of the Brahmaputra Board for flood management covering 
the rivers Brahmaputra, Barak and their major tributaries; 
(iv) formulation of the National Water Policy, 2002, which has recommended 
for the preparation of basin -wise Master Plans for flood management and 
control and for providing adequate flood cushion in the reservoir projects; 
(v) constitution of a Task Force in 2004 for Flood Management and Erosion 
Control in Assam and its neighboring States as well as Bihar, West 
Bengal and Eastern Uttar Pradesh. The report of the Task Force been 
circulated to all the concerned States and Central Ministries.

Statement 
Main Parameters laid down for grant of Swatantrata Sainik Samman Pension and 
instructions issued by the Government from time to time. 
(i) Eligibility Criteria: The following categories of freedom fighter s are eligible 
for the Samman Pension: 
(a) Eligible dependents of martyrs; 
(b) A person who had suffered minimum imprisonment of six months 
on account of participation in freedom struggle; 
(c) A persons who on account of his participation in freedom struggle 
remained underground for more than six months; 
(d) A person who, on account of participation in the freedom struggle, 
was interned in his home or externed from his district for a 
minimum period of 6 months; 
(e) A person whose property was confiscated or attached and sold due 
to participation in the freedom struggle; 
(f) A person who, on account of participation in freedom struggle, 
became permanently incapacitated during firing or lathi charge; 
(g) A person who lost his Govt. job for participation in freedom 
struggle; 
(h) A person who was awarded the punishment of 10 strokes of 
caning/flogging/whipping due to his participation in freedom 
struggle. 
(ii) Dependents: Spouses (widows/widowers), unmarried and unemployed 
daughters (up-to maximum three) and parents of deceased freedom figh ters (as 
also of martyrs) are eligible for grant of dependent family pension under the 
scheme. 
(iii) Special Dispensation For Women And Weaker Sections of the Society: The 
eligibility criteria for grant of pension on grounds of jail suffering specifies a 
minimum period of six months which the freedom fighters should have 
undergone in connection with the freedom movement. However, as a special 
dispensation for women freedom fighters and for the freedom fighters belonging 
to Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tri bes, the minimum period has been kept at 
three months. Eligible dependents of deceased freedom fighters for grant of 
dependent family pension are spouses (widow/widower), unmarried and 
unemployed daughters (up- to three) and mother and father. Sons of freed om 
fighters have not been recognized as eligible dependents. 
(iv) Evidence and procedure in case of Jail Suffering: Any applicant who claims 
jail suffering should submit the following evidence in support of his claim: 

108   Written Answers to [RAJYA SABHA] Unstarred Questions 
(a) Primary Evidence:Imprisonment/detention certificate from the 
concerned jail authority, District Magistrate or the State 
Government indicating the period of sentence awarded, date of 
admission, date of release, facts of the case and reasons for release. 
(b) Secondary Evidence:In case records of the relevant period are not 
available, secondary evidence in the form of 2 co -prisoner 
certificates (CPCs) from freedom fighters who have proven jail 
suffering of minimum 1 year and who were with the  applicant in the 
jail could be considered provided the State Government/ Union 
Territory Administration concerned, after due verification of the 
claim and its genuineness, certifies that the documentary evidence 
from the official records in support of the  claimed suffering are not 
available. In case the certifier happens to be a sitting or ex. 
M.P/M.L.A., only one certificate in place of the two is required. 
(v) Evidence and procedure in case of underground suffering: Any applicant who 
claims underground suffering should submit the following evidence in support of 
his claim: 
(a) Primary evidence:Documentary evidence by way of Court’s/ 
Government’s orders proclaiming the applicant as an absconder, 
announcing an award on his head or for his arrest or ordering his  
detention. According to the Swatantrata Sainik Samman Pension 
Scheme, 1980, absconsion on issue of warrant of arrest is not an 
eligible suffering for grant of Samman pension unless the same is 
followed by the order of proclaimed offender/or award for arre st/on 
head or detention order. 
(b) Secondary evidence:In the absence of primary record -based 
evidence, a Non -availability or Records Certificate (NARC) from 
the concerned State Government/Union territory Administration 
along with a Personal Knowledge Certificate (PKC) from a 
prominent freedom fighter who has proven jail suffering of a 
minimum two years and who happened to be from the same 
administrative district can be submitted as supporting evidence to 
the claim. 
(vi) Non -Availability of Records Certificate ( NARC):Where records of the 
relevant period are not available, a Non -Availability of Records Certificate 
(NARC) from the concerned authority is a mandatory pre- requisite for secondary 
evidence. 
(vii) Verification report of State Government:The claims of Cen tral Samman 
pension can be considered by the Central Government only when these are duly 
verified and recommended by the State Governments/Union Territory 
Administrations concerned in accordance with the provisions of the Scheme.

Rehabilitation of undertrials 
†1759. SHRI SURENDRA LATH: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the State-wise details of the total number of undertrials imprisoned in different 
jails in the country; 
(b) whether it is a fact that there are large number of such prisoners who are 
languishing in jails for years as they are not in a position to provide bail-surety; 
(c) whether Government have formulated any policy for the welfare and 
rehabilitation of such prisoners; 
(d) whether it is also a fact that more prisoners are kept almost in all the jails than 
their respective capacities and no proper arrangement is made with regard to their food, 
lodging and sleeping; and 
(e) if so, whether Government are formulating any plan in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI 
MANIKRAO GAVIT): (a) As per statistics compiled by the National Crime Records 
Bureau, there were 237076 undertrials detained in various jails of the country as on 
31.12.2005. The State-wise details of undertrails is given in Statement-I (See below). 
(b) A Statement indicating the number of undertrial prisoners kept in jails for 
various period at the end of 2005 is at Statement-II (See below). 
(c) to (e) ‘‘Prisons’’ is a State subject under List II of the Seventh Schedule to the 
Constitution of India and Prison Administration is primarily the responsibility of the 
respective State Governments. However, with a view to supplement the efforts of the 
State Governments the following reform measures have  been taken up by the Central 
Government: 
 
(1) In order to improve the condition of prisons, prisoners and the prison staff, 
the Central Government launched a non -plan scheme in 2002- 03 for 
construction of additional prisons to reduce overcrowding, repair and 
renovation of existing prisons, improvement in sanitation and prison staff. 
The scheme is being implemented over a period of five years with an 
outlay of Rs 1800 crore on cost sharing basis in the ratio of 75:25 between 
the Central and State Governments respectively. 
(2) A new section viz. 436A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 has been 
inserted in the Code to provide that where an undertrial prisoner other than 
the one accused on an offence for which death has been prescribed as one 
of the punishments, has been under detention for a period extending to one -
half of the maximum period of imprisonment, provided for the alleged 
offence, he should be released on his personal bond, with or without 
sureties. It also provides that in no case will an undertrial pr isoner be 
detained beyond the maximum period of imprisonment for which he can be 
convicted for the alleged offence. 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 

110   Written Answers to [RAJYA SABHA] Unstarred Questions 
Section 436 (1) of the C ode of Criminal Procedure, 1973 has also 
been amended to make a mandatory provision that if the arrested person is 
accused for a bailable offence and he is an indigent and cannot furnish 
surety, the Court shall release him on his execution of a bond without 
sureties. 
(3) In 2006, the Government of India has introduced the system of plea 
bargaining primarily to reduce pendency of cases in trial courts and 
overcrowding in prisons. Under plea bargaining an accused will be entitled 
to a reduced sentence if he admit s to the crime and agrees to compensate 
the victim. This will also require the consent of the victim, judge and 
prosecutor. The accused will have to file an application before the judge for 
plea bargaining. 
(4) For disposal of long pending sessions and other cases, Government of India 
has also set up 1562 Fast Track Court which have disposed off a total of 
10.4 lakh cases out of 18.2 cases transferred to them. 
(5) Government of India has prepared a Model Prison Manual and circulated to 
all the State Governments/Union Territories in December, 2003 for their 
guidance. The manual aims at bringing in basic uniformity in laws, rules 
and regulations governing the administration of prisons and the 
management of prisoners all over the country; rationalisation of prison 
practices to cater effectively to various categories of prisoners, spelling out 
minimum standards of institutional services for the care, protection, 
treatment, education, training and resocialisation of incarcerated offenders 
etc.

Alternative means to start peace talks with ULFA 
1772. SHRI URKHAO GWRA BRAHMA: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government has declined to continue the  
intermediary peace initiative, initiated by renowned writer Jnanpith Award winner  
Dr. Indira Goswamy for peaceful settlement with ULFA; 
(b) if so, whether Government will have alternative means and ways to restart the 
peace process; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that other insurgent groups like National Democratic 
Front of Bodoland have passed two years of ceasefire but no discussion has been held to 
settle their issues; and 

Written Answers to [29 AUG., 2007] Unstarred Questions   131 
(d) if so, when is the formal discussion likely to be held? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFA IRS 
(SHRIMATI V. RADHIKA SELVI): (a) and (b) Dr. Indira Goswami had earlier taken 
the initiative for talks with United Liberation Front of Asom (ULFA). After three 
rounds of talks with Peoples' Consultative Group (PCG), which was set up by ULFA, 
Government had declared unilateral Suspension of Operations (SoO) by Army against 
ULFA from 13.8.2006 to 20.9.2006 with a view to create a conducive atmosphere for 
holding of peace talks. There was no direct response from ULFA and some inputs were 
received of regrou ping, new raising, violence, collection of weapons/explosives and 
extortion by ULFA cadres. As a result, Counter Insurgency operations against ULFA 
were resumed. 
Dr. Indira Goswami in the capacity of President Nagrik Shanti Manch (NSM) 
recently presented a memorandum for resumption of peace talks between Centre/ State 
Government and ULFA. Dr. Indira Goswami has been, inter alia , informed that the 
Government would await a formal communication from top ULFA leaders indicating 
their willingness to enter into n egotiations without any pre -conditions. Response is yet 
to be received from ULFA leaders. 
(c) and (d) Suspension of Operations (SoO) agreement is in force with National 
Democratic Front of Bodoland (NDFB) since 1.6.2005. The NDFB has been repeatedly 
requested to submit its Charter of Demands so that discussions could be initiated but 
they have not submitted its Charter of Demands so far. It is, therefore, premature to 
indicate the time frame for formal talks with NDFB. 
Persons killed/injured by blueline buses in Delhi 
1773. SHRI RAJEEV CHANDRASEKHAR: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS 
be pleased to state: 
(a) the number of blue line private buses which were plying in Delhi as on 1st July, 
2007, number out of them which were more than eight years old; 
(b) whether a large number of these buses were not road worthy but were plying 
only by bribing officials and large number of complaints against them went un-heeded; 
(c) the number of persons killed and seriously injured by these buses during 2005-
06 and 2007, so far; 
(d) whether any ex-gratia payment is made in such cases; 
(e) if so, the details thereof; and 
(f) the action taken against concerned owners/crew? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRIMATI V. RADHlKA SELVI): (a) A total of 3871 Blue Line Stage Carriage 
permits were valid as on 1.7.2007 out of which buses more than eight years old are 441. 
(b) No, Sir.

blue line priva te buses during the years 2005, 2006 and 2007 (upto 15.8.2007) are as 
under:–

(d) and (e) Under the Motor Vehicles Act, a Solatium Fund Scheme (Hit and Run)

Non-adherence to TRAI norms by ZEE Telefilms 
1774. SHRI GIREESH KUMAR SANGHI: Will the Minister of INFORMATION 
AND BROADCASTING be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Zee Telefilms are not adhering to the norms to TRAI  
in providing their bouquet of channels to Tata Sky and Doordarshan; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that viewers to Tata Sky and Doordarshan are unable to 
watch the Zee channels; and 
(c) if so, the steps Government have taken or propose to take to ensure that Zee 
Telefilms adhere to TRAI norms and provide their bouquet of channels to Tata Sky and 
Doordarshan? 
THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING (SHRI 
PRIYARANJAN DASMUNSI): (a) TRAI has not prescribed any norms for provision 
of specific bouquet or specific channel by a broadcaster to a DTH service provider. 
However, clause 3.2 of TRAI’s Interconnection regulation of 10th December, 2004 has 
provided for non-discriminatory access to all distributors of TV channels. 
(b) Carrying any particular channel o n DTH platform is purely a business and 
commercial decision of a DTH service provider. TRAI has not mandated the carriage of 
specific channels on different DTH platforms. 
(c) In view of reply to part (a) and (b), the question does not arise.

Support to Indian films for tapping overseas markets 
1775. SHRIMATI HEMA MALINI: Will the Minister of INFORMATION AND 
BROADCASTING be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Govemment are aware that Indian film makers are pois ed to increase 
their shares across the world and also planning to tap newer, overseas markets in the 
US, UK and South East Asia; 
(b) if so, whether it is a fact that there is emerging global markets for Indian films;  
(c) if so, whether Government is prepared to ex tend encouraging and needful 
support to Indian film makers; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; and 
(e) if not, the reasons therefore? 
THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING (SHRI 
PRIYARANJAN DASMUNSI): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. The growing Indian diaspora 
around the world has created a market for Indian films overseas that continues to grow 
at a rapid rate. As per the Price Water House Coopers Report of 2007 conducted by 
FICCI, the overseas market is currently estimated to be worth Rs.700 crores in 2006 and 
is expected to grow at a Compound Annual Growth Rate of 18%. It is expected to reach 
Rs. 850 crores during 2007. In accordance with the feed back received from 
representatives of Indian Film Industry, markets for Indian film are growing steadily in 
North Europe, G ermany, France and Japan. In China too, there is huge untapped film 
market. Recently, the mainstream cable companies in the United States have started a 
‘‘Video on Demand’’ for Indian films. Latin America is also considered as a new 
market for Indian films. 
(c) and (d) Recognising the potential of export of Indian films abroad, Government 
of India has taken several steps to encourage promotion of Indian films. They are as 
follows: 
(i) To promote Indian films, Government of India through its Plan Scheme 
‘‘Participation in foreign Film Festival/Markets’’, encourages Indian 
companies and producers to participate in global film festivals and 
markets such as Cannes Film Festival/Market, American Film Market, 
MIPCOM, etc. Further, in order to promote cinema, Gover nment of India 
is spreading awareness and to enhance the visibility of our film industry 
by organizing India pavilion in number of film markets, screening of 
Indian films, in different International film festivals. Indian film festivals 
are also organized in different countries regularly. 
(ii) Audio -visual co -production agreements have been signed with Republic of 
Italy, United Kingdom, Brazil and Germany and similar proposals with 
other countries are being explored to expand revenues of finances and 
markets to the Indian film industry. 
(iii) In order to ensure all round development of film industry, five Core Groups, 
comprising of the representatives of the film industry, have 

134   Written Answers to [RAJYA SABHA] Unstarred Questions 
been constituted to s ubmit its suggestions on measures to promote the 
film industry. A Core Group on ‘‘Export of Films and Related Issues’’ 
has submitted its recommendations and action is being taken. 
(iv) Efforts are being made to ensure constitution of Export Promotion 
Forum/Council by the film industry. Such Forum, as and when

Labour law for women working in night shifts 
1785. DR. VIJAY MALLYA: Will the Minister of LABOUR AND EMPLOYMENT 
be pleased to state: 
(a) what are the labour laws in respect of women working in night shifts; 
(b) what are the jobs that are restricted to women during night shifts; 
(c) whether the women working in night shifts get additional compensation/ 
consideration as per law; and 
(d) whether Government propose to amend the law considering the increase in 
number of women working for Information Technology sector? 
THE MINISTER  OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR AND 
EMPLOYMENT (SHRI OSCAR FERNANDES): (a) and (b) Sections 51 to 66 under 
the Factories Act, 1948 contain provisions relating to the working hours of adults 
(including women). As per Clause (b) of Sub -Section (1) of Sec tion 66, no woman is 
required or allowed to work in any factory except between the hours of 6 A.M. and 7 
P.M. 
The State Governments are empowered to vary these time limits by notification in 
the official Gazette in respect of any factory or group or class or description of factories. 
However, no variation would permit the employment of any woman between the hours 
of 10 P.M. and 5 A.M. The State Governments are also empowered to make rules 
providing exemptions from these restrictions in respect of women work ing in fish 
curing or fish canning factories, subject to certain conditions. 
(c) The Factories Act and the Rules framed thereunder do not contain  
provisions relating to additional compensation to be given to women working  
during night. However, while allow ing employment of women workers in night in  
fish curing or fish canning factories State Government is empowered to put certain  
conditions, relating to additional welfare and security measures, such as: 
(i) free transport during night hours 
(ii) creche and food/snacks/tea facilities 
(iii) rest room and separate lockers 
(iv) placing of women workers in groups during night 
(v) night duty not continuously for more than one week. 
(d) The Government of India has introduced an amendment to Section 66 of the  
Factories Act, 1948 vide Bill No. 104 of 2005 in the Lok Sabha for allowing women  
to work in factories in night shifts, irrespective of type of industry. Information  
Technology units registered under the Factories Act, 1948 would also be covered 
by the proposed amendment.

Complete eradication of child labour 
1795. SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA: Will the Minister of LABOUR AND  
EMPLOYMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) by when the practice of child labour will be comp letely eradicated in our 
country; 
(b) whether Government propose to make the law more stringent; and 
(c) what special steps would be taken to discourage the practice, apart from banning 
the same in 2006? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR AND 
EMPLOYMENT (SHRI OSCAR FERNANDES): (a) Government is committed to the 
elimination of all forms of child labour. Child labour being a socio- economic problem is 
a result of poverty and illiteracy. Considering the magnitude and the nature of the 
problem, Government h as adopted a gradual and sequential approach to withdraw and 
rehabilitate working children, beginning with those working in hazardous 
occupations/processes and then covering children working in other occupations. In this 
direction, Government is implementing the National Child Labour Project (NCLP) 
Scheme in 250 districts of the country. 
(b) and (c) There are stringent provisions under the Child Labour (Prohibition and 
Regulation) Act, 1986. As per Section 14 of the Act, any person who employs a child in 
any occupation or process where employment of children is banned under the Act, is 
liable for punishment with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than 3 
months but which may extend to one year or with fine ranging from Rs. 10,000/ - to Rs. 
20,000/-. The quantum of punishment for a repeat offence is imprisonment for a term 
which shall not be less than 6 months but which may extend to two years. As the State 
Governments/UTs are appropriate Governments for enforcement of the Act, in their 
respective areas, directions are regularly being given to them for strict enforcement, 
creating public awareness on the issue and for effective implementation of the NCLP 
Scheme.

rural habitations as except for the States like Gujarat, Mizoram, Tamil Nadu and UT of 
Puducherry, most others have failed to achieve the targets that were set for them;

having water sources contaminated by chemicals, only 9,754 (about 5 per cent) have 
been provided safe alternatives; and 
(c) if so, the steps Government propose to take to make the programme a success?  
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT 
(SHRI CHANDRA SEKHAR SAHU): (a) to (c) Under Bharat Nirman, targets have 
been set for all States for four years, from 2005 -06 to 2008- 09 to cover 55067 
uncovered habitations, 3,31,604 habitations which have slipped back from full coverage 
and 2,16,968 habitations which have water quality problems. Target for each year to a 
State is set taking into account the coverage in the previous year, and any backlog is 
added for the forthcoming year. This ensures that the overall targets for Bharat Nirman 
period are met. 
As regards quality affected habitation, the States have reported coverage of 4550 
habitations during 2005- 06 and 5330 habitations during 2006- 07. During 2006- 07, 
another 23790 habitations have been sanctioned with projects, with the remaining such 
habitations being addressed in 2007- 08 and 2008- 09. In order to achieve these target, 
the States have been suggested to adopt cos t-effective local solutions through ground 
water recharge for in -situ dilution of contaminants, surface water harvesting structures 
like village ponds, Ooranies and roof -top rainwater harvesting structures. Cost effective 
Stand-alone systems are also to be adopted by the States with proper sludge/wastewater 
disposal. States have been specifically advised to prioritize addressing arsenic and 
fluoride problems as these contaminants cause long lasting ill-effects on human health.

154   Written Answers to [RAJYA SABHA] Unstarred Questions 
implementation of Total Sanitation Campaign, now over 45% households have access 
to toilets. 
(b) and (c) The Central Rural S anitation Programme (CRSP) has been restructured 
as the Total Sanitation Campaign (TSC) with a view to following a community led and 
people centered approach. The programme gives emphasis on Information, Education 
and Communication (lEC) for demand generat ion of sanitation facilities. The demand 
so generated is met through a wide range of technological choices suited to varying 
requirement of households in different income categories and hydrological conditions. It 
also lays emphasis on school sanitation an d hygiene education for bringing about 
attitudinal and behavioural changes for relevant sanitation and hygiene practices from 
young age. Government has also launched an incentive -cum-reward scheme viz. Nirmal

1807. SHRI JANARDHANA POOJARY: Will the Minister of RURAL

equivalent programme currently being implemented in the country; 
(b) the total allocation made and sanctioned for implementation of the above

(c) the terms and conditions, together with the rate of interest charged, applicable

(d) whether security/surety is required for availing the assistance under the above 
programme; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof; and if not, what action is taken against implementing 
agencies demanding security/surety from the beneficiaries? 
THE MINISTER OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI RAGHUVANSH PRASAD 
SINGH): (a) The Swarnjayanti Gram Swarojgar Yojana (SGSY), a holistic self -
employment generation programme; was launched with effect from 1st April, 1999 after 
restructuring the erstwhile IRDP (Integrated Rural Development Programme). The 
objective of SGSY is to bring the assisted poor families (swarojgaries) above the 
poverty line by ensuring appreciable increase in incomes over a period of time. This 
objective is to be achieved inter alia by organizing the rural poor into Self -Help Groups 
(SHGs) through a process of social mobilization, their training and capacity building 
and provision of income generating assets through a mix of bank credit and government 
subsidy. Funds under the SGSY are shared by the Central and the State Governments in 
the ratio of 75:25. The selection of activities under the scheme is based on the local 
resources, the aptitude and skill of the intended swarojgaries and market potential for 
products. The scheme focuses on vulnerable section of the society including women and 
socially challenged sections. As per the guidelines of the scheme, 50% of the group 
formed in each block should be exclusively for the women. Further, Women, SCs/STs 
and disabled a re to account for at least 40%,50% and 3% of the assisted swarojgaries 
respectively. 
(b) A Statement indicating State-wise and year-wise details of central allocation and 
releases made under the SGSY during the last five years is enclosed (See below). 
(c) to (e) F inancial assistance to swarojgaries under SGSY comprises of two 
components viz. loan and subsidy. SGSY is a credit -  linked scheme and credit is the 
key element. Subsidy is only a minor and enabling component. The size of loan for 
project depends on the na ture of the project. Interest rate for SGSY loans will be as 
notified by the Reserve Bank of India/National Bank for Agriculture and Rural 
Development from time to time. The security norms, as prescribed by the Reserve Bank 
of India from time to time will be applicable. The implementation of SGSY, including 
credit disbursement, is periodically monitored at Block, District, State and Central 
levels. Any grievance from the beneficiaries is referred to the Ministry of Finance and 
the concerned State Government for taking remedial measures.

Metalling of roads under PMGSY in Uttarakhand 
1808. SHRI RAJ NATH SINGH: Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that the State Government of Uttarakhand is not 
taking stringent action in regard to metalling of roads which were constructed under the 
PMGSY scheme;

metalling of these roads which were constructed 10 years back for the convenience of 
the villagers; and

THE MINISTER OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI RAGHUVANSH PRASAD 
SINGH): (a) Under Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY), rural roads projects 
are executed by the State Government. The programme is implemented in accordance 
with programme guidelines which, inter-alia, provide that in hill States, the estimate for 
new construction works may be prepared in 2 parts wherever circumstances so require. 
As such, the 1st stage would consist of formation cutting, slope stabilization, protection 
works and drainage works. If black topping at the s econd stage is intended, it may be 
taken up after two rainy seasons have elapsed to ensure adequate stabilization of the 
side slopes. The second stage will include the WBM (Water Bound Macadam) layers 
and bituminous surface course. 
(b) and (c) The existing  guidelines provided for up gradation of existing rural roads 
core net work roads to the required structural and geometric standards. However, the 
first priority is to provide connectivity to unconnected eligible habitations.

1809. SHRI K.E. ISMAIL: 
SHRI SYED AZEEZ PASHA: 
Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that random inspection of road works under PMGSY during 
July, 2004 and September, 2006 has found substantial numbe r of works under the 
scheme, of unsatisfactory quality in several States; 
(b) if so, the details of the findings; and 
(c) the measures being taken to ensure quality of the road projects and check 
corruption in implementation of the projects under the PMGSY? 
THE MINISTER OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI RAGHUVANSH PRASAD 
SINGH): (a) and (b) During the period July, 2004 to September, 2006, a total of 17718 
inspections were carried out by the National Quality Monitors (NQMs) under the third 
tier of the quality control mechanism of Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY). 
Out of total 7449 inspection of completed works, 1547 works (21%) were graded as 
‘Unsatisfactory’, whereas out of 10269 inspections of on-

going works, 4309 works (42%) were graded as ‘Unsatisfactory’. State -wise details of

(c) For ensuring high level of quality in works, PMGSY programme guidelines have 
the provision for three tier Quality Control Mechanism. The first two tiers of the Quality 
Control Structure are overseen by the State Quality Coordinators, appointed by the State 
Governments. The first tier of quality control mechanism is in -house quality control at 
the level of the executing agencies. Field laboratories are established by the Contractors 
and mandatory tests on the quality of material and workmanship are conducted under 
the supervision of Programme Implementation Units (PIUs). The second tier provides 
for quality monitoring by the State Governments through independent State Quality

Land reforms in the country 
1812. SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of RURAL  
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the land reform process was incomplete in all States in the country; 
(b) if so, the States where land reforms completed fully as on date; 
(c) the details of such reforms, State-wise; 
(d) the States where land reforms are partially completed; 
(e) the reasons therefor; 
(f) the steps being taken by Government to complete the land reforms in each State;  
(g) whether Government had set any time-frame to complete these reforms; and 

Written Answers to [29 AUG., 2007] Unstarred Questions   167 
(h) if so, the details thereof, State-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI CHANDRA 
SEKHAR SAHU): (a) to (h) Land and its management falls within the administrative 
jurisdiction of the State Governments as provided under Entry No.18 of State List (List 
II) of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. The role of the Central Government in 
this field is only of an advisory and coordinating nature. However, implem entation of 
land reforms programmes is reviewed from time to time at various fora, including 
Conferences of the Revenue Ministers/Secretaries of States and UTs organized by the 
Ministry of Rural Development. While the task of abolition of intermediary tenu res and 
interests has been completed all over the country, the other aspects of the land reforms 
programmes, viz. tenancy reforms, distribution of ceiling surplus land, Government 
wasteland including Bhoodan land, special measures for protection of land of  Scheduled 
Castes and Tribes, consolidation of holdings, etc, are continuing in the States. 
As per the information received from the States, 125.85 lakh tenants have been 
conferred ownership rights or their rights are protected, covering an area of 167.16 lakh 
acres. On implementation of the land ceiling laws, an area of 68.91 lakh acres has been 
declared surplus, of which 60.53 lakh acres has been taken possession of, and 50.34 
lakh acres has been distributed to 54.05 lakh beneficiaries, of whom 39 per cen t belong 
to Scheduled Castes and 16 per cent to Scheduled Tribes. In addition, 153.22 lakh acres 
of Government wasteland, and 16.66 lakh acres of Bhoodan land, have been distributed 
to the eligible rural poor. Further, an area of 1739.01 lakh acres has bee n consolidated. 
An area of 4.18 lakh acres of alienated tribal land has been restored to the tribals.  
Government of India has not set any time -frame for completion of land reforms in 
the country. However, the status of implementation of the land reforms sc hemes/ 
programmes was reviewed during the Conference of the Revenue Secretaries of the 
States and UTs held in New Delhi on 7th June, 2006 under the Chairmanship of 
Minister of Rural Development. The need for effective implementation of various 
components/schemes of land reforms was stressed in the Conference, so that the 
benefits reach the grass roots level. Thereafter, Minister (RD) had written to the Chief 
Ministers of the States for having a thorough review of the implementation of the land 
reforms programmes and schemes, so as to help in the planning and formulation of the 
Eleventh Five Year Plan. They had been requested to conduct special drives for 
implementation of the land reforms programmes, including tenancy reforms; 
distribution of ceiling surplus  land, Government wasteland and Bhoodan land, 
homestead land; prevention of alienation of tribal land and their restoration, so that the 
number of landless and homesteadless families in the country could be reduced. He had 
also separately written to the Ch ief Ministers for undertaking a special drive to get the 
court cases involving ceiling surplus lands disposed of, especially the cases pending in 
Revenue Courts on which State Govts. have control. They have also been requested to 
consider setting up of Land Tribunals under Article 323-B of the Constitution or Special 
Benches in the High Courts for speedy disposal of the pending cases. 
Thus, the States are being pursued for vigorous implementation of land reforms.
